1.title: Why Use a Geological Classification Instead of a Regional Map?
1.html:
The Alsatian geologist Claude Sittler proposed a classification centred on the origin of rocks and soils, grouping the 51 Grand Crus by geological character into ten families. The classification matters because it can truly explain "why" a site suits a certain variety and produces a certain style — rather than merely memorising place names.

For example: granite sites are naturally suited to Riesling showing minerality and backbone; marl-limestone tends to nurture full-structured Gewurztraminer. This is the organising logic of all the Level 2 lessons that follow.
2.title: The Ten Geological Families at a Glance (Number of Grand Crus)
2.items.0.label: Schist (1)
2.items.0.desc: Kastelberg — Silurian Steige schist, metamorphosed by Andlau granite, a hard, dark rock
2.items.1.label: Volcano-sedimentary (2)
2.items.1.desc: Muenchberg, Rangen — Permian volcanic-clastic rock and true volcanic rock, the only volcanic geology in Alsace
2.items.2.label: Granite (8)
2.items.2.desc: Schlossberg, Brand, Sommerberg etc. — sandy soils weathered from Vosges two-mica granite
2.items.3.label: Sandstone / Vosges sandstone (3)
2.items.3.desc: Wiebelsberg, Kessler, Kitterlé — cemented quartz sand, well-drained and quick to warm
2.items.4.label: Limestone (4)
2.items.4.desc: Bruderthal, Rosacker, Steinert, Steinklotz — Muschelkalk / Dogger limestone bedrock
2.items.5.label: Calcareous sandstone (3)
2.items.5.desc: Geisberg, Pfingstberg, Zinnkoepflé — Triassic calcareous sandstone; Zinnkoepflé is even the "roof of the Alsace vineyards"
2.items.6.label: Marl-sandstone (7)
2.items.6.desc: Furstentum, Pfersigberg, Vorbourg etc. — one of the largest subgroups in this course
2.items.7.label: Marl-limestone-sandstone (4)
2.items.7.desc: Altenberg de Bergheim, Engelberg, Osterberg, Zotzenberg — one of the two blended Grand Crus is here
2.items.8.label: Marl-limestone (13, the largest family)
2.items.8.desc: Eichberg, Hengst, Mambourg etc. — more than a quarter of all Grand Crus belong to this type
2.items.9.label: Clay-marl (5)
2.items.9.desc: Schoenenbourg, Kanzlerberg, Sporen etc. — heavy, water-retaining soils that nurture powerful noble-rot sweet wines
3.question: According to Claude Sittler's geological classification, which geological family has the most of the 51 Grand Crus?
3.options.1: Marl-limestone (13) — more than a quarter of all Grand Crus belong to this type
3.explanation: The marl-limestone (marno-calcaires) family has 13 Grand Crus, the largest of the ten families, including well-known sites such as Eichberg, Florimont, Goldert, Hatschbourg, Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr, Mambourg, Mandelberg, Marckrain, Moenchberg, Sonnenglanz, Steingrubler and Altenberg de Wolxheim.
4.message: Sittler's geological classification complete! Next we explore the 51 Grand Crus one by one within this framework.
4.keyPoints.0: Claude Sittler grouped the 51 Grand Crus into ten geological families by rock and soil origin
4.keyPoints.1: Family sizes differ widely: schist has only 1 (Kastelberg), marl-limestone as many as 13
4.keyPoints.2: Geological classification explains "why" rather than merely "memorising place names" — the key method for understanding terroir
4.keyPoints.3: All later Level 2 lessons follow this ten-family framework
